metadata.title: The Hexagonality Law in Real Materials II: Entropy and Pressure
metadata.description:
The Hexagonality Law (#66) says that in ideal stackings every kind of piece is a straight line in the share h of hexagonal layers; in the physicists' layer model this is a property with only a nearest term (#68). DICTO proposed to test the law's form on two quantities that decide which stacking a crystal takes: its entropy and its enthalpy under pressure. Entropy: Mau and Huse wrote the stacking entropy of hard spheres in the same layer model; at close packing their nearest term is 55 and the next 6 (in 10⁻⁵ kB per sphere), so the entropy is about 90% of the law's form, and the farther terms grow toward melting (37, 18 and 9). Pressure: we prove that if a crystal's volume follows the law's form, pressure shifts only the balance between cubic and hexagonal layers and never reorders the longer stackings among themselves, and that it keeps the fault ratios 2 : 2 : 1. From published volumes and energies, at first order, pressure strengthens cubic 3C silicon carbide against 6H, 4H and 2H, as experiments find (6H turns into 3C above about 4.5 GPa); in silicon and germanium, whose volumes bend away from the straight line, pressure tilts them toward hexagonal-type stackings, mainly through the farther term.

The proposition is proved in the paper; all material data are published values (sources listed); the pressure estimate is first order.

The ideas and names are DICTO's. Computation and proof with Claude (Anthropic). Sources checked are listed in the paper. The studies (scripts and results) are attached. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com.

metadata.title: The Hexagonality Law and the Fibonacci Stacking: the Golden Ratio in the Volumes of a Never-Repeating Crystal
metadata.description:
DICTO's long-standing aim is a bridge between repeating and never-repeating order. Close-packed layers can be stacked in a never-repeating Fibonacci order: layer types cubic (c) and hexagonal (h) following the substitution c → ch, h → c. We prove that in this stacking the share of hexagonal layers is exactly 1/φ² and that hexagonal layers never touch, so of the four kinds of piece between neighbouring layers only three occur, in the golden proportions 1/φ³ : 1/φ² : 1/φ² (cubic–cubic, cubic–hexagonal, hexagonal–cubic). By the Hexagonality Law (#66), every kind of piece then averages exactly V(cc) + (V(hh) − V(cc))/φ² per layer: the golden ratio enters the volumes of a crystal exactly. In rock salt at weight λ = 1/3 the ball piece averages 10999/20736 − (71/6912)√5 per layer. The Fibonacci order closes into periodic stackings of 15, 16, 26 and 63 layers with hexagonalities 2/5, 3/8, 5/13 and 8/21, ratios of Fibonacci numbers. On the first three, the Laves phases keep the law exactly in all 90 tests, including the foot atom for which the law is not proved. The stackings in which hexagonal layers never touch are exactly the configurations of the supersymmetric lattice fermions of Fendley, Schoutens and de Boer, whose ground states have the hexagonality of 6H.

Version 2 adds the 26-layer approximant (the law exact in all 90 tests) and a section on hard-core supersymmetric fermions (Fendley, Schoutens and de Boer).

The theorem is proved in the paper; the Laves walks are exact (rational arithmetic, #57's census engine), the law tested as polynomial identities.

The ideas and names are DICTO's. Computation and proof with Claude (Anthropic). Sources checked are listed in the paper. The study (scripts, exact results, the new weight walks) is attached. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com.

metadata.title: DICTO: Collected Geometric Works
metadata.description:
DICTO is a geometric sculptor in Osaka. The work grows out of building with recycled PET bottles and from three open apps on one shared geometry: Kaleidohedra, Rhombiverse and Polyhedraverse.

This record gathers all of DICTO's published geometry in one place. It opens with a short essay, Quanta of Space, which reads the works as a study of the pieces from which space is built, from the atoms of the ancients (Democritus, Plato's Timaeus) to the quanta of modern physics (loop quantum gravity), and as a bridge between periodic and aperiodic order. The papers follow in four chapters: Atoms (new solids), Bonds (how pieces fill space), Shells (layers round a core) and Cycles (rules that turn one shell into the next). metadata.title: Real Polytypes and the Hexagonality Law: Silicon Carbide, Silicon, Germanium and Cerium against the Straight Line
metadata.description:
The Hexagonality Law (#66) says that in ideal stackings every kind of piece totals a straight line in the share h of hexagonal layers. DICTO proposed to test it against real crystals. In the language physicists use for stackings, the axial Ising (ANNNI) model, we prove that a property is a straight line in h exactly when its couplings between layers two and three apart vanish, J2 = J3 = 0, and that its stacking faults then stand intrinsic : extrinsic : twin = 2 : 2 : 1, the ratios of #67. We then read published data. The computed volumes of the silicon carbide polytypes lie on the line within the precision of the published numbers; the measured ones scatter between laboratories by more than the whole effect. Silicon and germanium bend slightly but clearly, by about 0.04% of the volume: their volume couplings J2 are of the size of J1, a relaxation that ideal geometry does not have. Germanium's stacking-fault energies come close to the ideal 2 : 2 : 1 (2.25 : 2.06 : 1), silicon's do not (4.1 : 2.4 : 1). Silicon carbide's band gap is far from straight. In cerium, the double-hexagonal form at h = 1/2 has 1.2% more volume than the cubic form. The straight line is the ideal part of every stacking; the departures measure what real crystals add.

The proposition is proved in the paper; all crystal data are published values (sources listed), fitted with short scripts attached in the study.

The ideas and names are DICTO's. Computation and proof with Claude (Anthropic). Sources checked are listed in the paper. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com.

metadata.title: Random Stackings and Stacking Faults: the Hexagonality Law at Work
metadata.description:
The Hexagonality Law (#66) says that in a stacking of close-packed layers, where space is shared out by weight among atoms and holes, each kind of piece totals exactly what its layers hold in their own pure stackings. DICTO proposed to look for the conditions where this matters in real matter. Two follow at once, and both are exact. Theorem 1 (any stacking): however the layers are stacked, repeating, faulted or random, with any correlations, each kind of piece averages exactly V(cc) + h·(V(hh) − V(cc)) per layer, where h is the share of hexagonal layers; so the single number that diffraction measures in randomly stacked colloids and in stacking-disordered ice fixes every hole volume exactly. Theorem 2 (faults): a stacking fault changes the total of every kind of piece by exactly the number of layers it turns hexagonal (or cubic) times V(hh) − V(cc); the classical faults of cubic crystals (twin, intrinsic, extrinsic) turn 1, 2 and 2 layers hexagonal, those of hexagonal crystals (I1, I2, E) turn 1, 2 and 3 layers cubic. In rock salt the balls gain at each fault exactly what the holes lose. The one piece the law's proof does not cover, the Laves foot atom that reads three layers, keeps the law exactly on every stacking up to eight layers (390 of 390 exact tests).

Proofs from the Hexagonality Law (#66); fault layer counts by Jagodzinski's rule on the classical sequences; rock salt values exact in rational arithmetic; the Laves test walks nine further stackings of seven and eight layers exactly with #57's census engine.

Version 2 adds three figures: the pieces of rock salt and nickel arsenide (not to scale), the exact straight line for the diamond / ice framework with measured stacking-disordered ice, and the six classical faults as strips of layers.

The ideas and names are DICTO's. Computation and proof with Claude (Anthropic). Sources checked are listed in the paper. The study (scripts, exact results, the new weight walks) is attached. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com.

metadata.description:
Exact geometry of the named polyhedra found or named by DICTO (artist, Osaka) in his published papers and the Kaleidohedra findings archive: 62 solids, among them the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron, the DICTO Hecatodihedron, the DICTO OG family, the DBT and OTT, the DICTO Jewel, the six DICTONIC SOLIDS of #48 and #51, the twelve solids of version 3 (#55, #56, #57, #59) Ganesha (#61 The Swap Rule: the Janus c/h tetrahedral piece of a squashed stacking, at the paper's Figure 1 parameters ACBC, layer spacing² = (3/4)(2/3), λ = 1/10; in ℚ(√3)), Shadow-17 (#62 Shadows of the Fourth Dimension: a new construction from a known piece, two J11, Johnson's gyroelongated pentagonal pyramid, glued on their pentagons, the equal-edged form of the 600-cell's outer edge-first slices; in ℚ(√5)) and Humpty Dumpty (#63 The White Queen 600-cell: the real 48-vertex cell-first slice of the 600-cell, a convex egg of 92 triangles with tetrahedral symmetry; in ℚ(√5)). New in version 5: eighteen named slices of the two four-dimensional queens, with DICTO's names: from #63 The White Queen 600-cell the Lion, Jabberwock, Tweedledum, Tweedledee, Mad Hatter, March Hare, Jubjub, Alicia, Alice, White Rabbit, Unicorn and Bandersnatch, and from #65 The Red Queen 120-cell Haigha, Hatta, the Red King, the Walrus, the Red Knight and the White Knight (D87–D101 for the fifteen new ones; Alicia, the Unicorn and the Bandersnatch are sections in Alicia Boole Stott's 1900 series, so known shapes; Humpty Dumpty's status is corrected to known for the same reason, D85 kept). Every coordinate is exact, in ℚ, ℚ(√3), ℚ(√5), ℚ(∛2) or ℚ(t) (t the root of an irreducible cubic, stated with its isolating interval), and also given to 15 decimals; each solid comes with its faces (consistently wound), f-vector, exact volume, squared edge lengths, symmetry group and the values stated in its paper, as JSON and OFF, plus a copy scaled to volume 1.

Also included: 6 packings that fill space and 4 published packings that do not, each with exact lattice vectors and exact placements of its pieces; and an inventory (index.csv) of all 137 rows of shapes DICTO has named, with finding number, paper, status (new, rediscovered or known), prior art and a universal number: established catalogue numbers (Johnson, uniform, Wenninger, Hart, Mosseri–Sadoc) where they exist, and DICTO's own permanent catalogue numbers D1–D86 for his new shapes, in order of first publication (version 4: D84 Ganesha, D85 Humpty Dumpty, D86 Shadow-17).

A standalone checker (check.py, Python 3 + sympy) re-proves every stated value from the data files alone: 1062 checks, all passing, including closed outward-wound surfaces, exact planarity, convexity where stated, symmetry, the non-convex keyed solids as convex pieces minus or plus Tricaps, and exact separating planes showing that the pieces of each packing do not overlap.

metadata.description:
DICTO concluded that "everything is the same study now: all aspects of everything we have been looking at have come to a focus". This paper sets out that focus: one map of how the threads of the recent papers meet, with the status of every link, and one new theorem that ties the flat stackings together. Stack equal balls in layers, each layer cubic or hexagonal by its neighbours, and share space out among the balls and the holes between them by weight, as real crystals do. The Hexagonality Law: in every stacking, each kind of piece totals exactly what its layers would hold in their own pure stackings, so the total is a straight line in the number of hexagonal layers, whatever their order. We prove it from the Swap Rule (#61) wherever a piece is fixed by its two neighbouring layers, show that it is equivalent to the Swap Rule there, and check it exactly in 1064 cases across pyrochlore, rock salt, cadmium iodide, zinc blende and the Laves phases, with no failure; in cadmium iodide, whose filled and empty layers alternate, it holds for each kind of layer separately. It holds even for the one Laves piece that reads three layers, where it is not yet proved. In the physics of stacking variants, straight-line laws in the hexagonality have been measured for sixty years; this is an exact geometric law of that form.

Proof: the Hexagonality Law is proved from the Swap Rule (and shown equivalent to it) wherever a piece is fixed by its two neighbouring layers; exact check (sympy, rational arithmetic) on the weight walks of #60 and #64, every close-packed stacking up to six layers, 1064 tests, none failing. The paper also maps every thread of the recent papers with its status. DICTO's radial cell projection (Polyhedraverse) is listed as his independent rediscovery of the classical reflection construction (Coxeter), made when he did not yet know it; no priority is claimed.

Version 2 corrects the wording of the radial cell projection row: an independent rediscovery.

The ideas and names are DICTO's. Computation and proof with Claude (Anthropic). Sources checked are listed in the paper. The study (scripts, exact results, the weight walks used) is attached. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com.

metadata.title: The Red Queen 120-cell: Aristotle's five pyramids as the cores of the regular four-dimensional solids
metadata.description:
Aristotle wrote that among solids the pyramid fills space, and the pyramids cut from the centres of the five Platonic solids have been argued over ever since. We prove that all five of these pyramids are the cores of the regular four-dimensional solids, seen in perspective: the tetrahedron, octahedron and icosahedron pyramids are the shadows of the cells round one corner of the 5-cell, the 16-cell and the 600-cell, and the cube, octahedron and dodecahedron pyramids are the shadows of the sides of the four-dimensional pyramid over one cell of the tesseract, the 24-cell and the 120-cell. Each shadow has exactly the proportions of Aristotle's pyramid, and the five come in polar pairs. The 120-cell, polar of the White Queen 600-cell of #63 and named the Red Queen by DICTO, is built exactly from the White Queen: its 600 corners are her 600 cell centres, its corners stand in her fifteen Cleo shells, its 120 dodecahedra in nine layers round one, and its core is the dodecahedron cut into twelve pentagonal pyramids where hers is the icosahedron cut into twenty Cleo-Icos. No convex regular solid has dodecahedra round a corner, but the star polytope {5/2,5,3} does: its twelve golden spikes at a corner cast exactly Aristotle's dodecahedron pyramids. Her full atlas is exact: 124 slice patterns in the four main directions, passing cell-first through the Archimedean solids of the icosahedral family, and four shadows, each filled exactly once by its front cells and once by its back cells, each the polar of the White Queen's middle slice.

1. From the White Queen to the Red Queen

In #63, the White Queen 600-cell, 600 regular tetrahedra stand round 120 corners, and round one corner they fall into fifteen shells whose core is twenty Cleo-Icos filling a regular icosahedron (#19, #44). DICTO proposed her polar swap: every corner of one solid becomes a cell of the other. The polar of the 600-cell is the 120-cell, 120 regular dodecahedra round 600 corners. DICTO named it the Red Queen, after the other queen of Through the Looking-Glass. He then proposed that the dodecahedral pyramid, the one of Aristotle's five pyramids the White Queen lacks, sits at the Red Queen's core, and that all five pyramids are four-dimensional shadows. They are.

Proof: exact arithmetic in ℚ(√5) throughout (rational pairs a+b√5): the 120-cell built from the exact 600-cell of #63 (13 of 13 checks), the five-pyramids theorem (10 of 10), the atlas (17 of 17). Both layer lists of the Red Queen (cells 1, 12, 20, 12, 30, 12, 20, 12, 1; corners in the fifteen Cleo shells) are palindromes, as the White Queen's shells are.

Version 2 follows an independent review of #63: it gives the four direction vectors and the exact checks of the atlas, reports Alicia Boole Stott's 1900 paper (On certain series of sections of the regular four-dimensional hypersolids; her 120-cell series is cell-first through the corner layers), tabulates all 124 slice patterns in an appendix, and states that the study files are attached.

The ideas and names are DICTO's. Computation and proof with Claude (Anthropic). Sources checked are listed in the paper. The study (scripts, data, renders) is attached. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com.

metadata.title: The White Queen 600-cell: an Exact Atlas of the Slices and Shadows of the 600-cell, and its Fifteen Cleo Shells
metadata.description:
The 600-cell is the four-dimensional solid built from 600 regular tetrahedra, twenty round every vertex. DICTO proposed a definitive, proved picture of it. We give a complete exact atlas of its three-dimensional slices in its four main directions, computed in numbers a + b√5. Between two neighbouring vertex heights a slice keeps one pattern of faces, so the cuts at the vertex heights and one cut inside each gap give every slice pattern: 62 on one side of the centre. Exactly twelve are made only of triangles. Every four-sided face is explained: the 46 squares are the equators of the regular octahedra inside the cells, and the 104 kites come from cells sitting symmetrically but tilted across the cut. Each of the four shadows resolves exactly into two halves, its front cells and its back cells, each filling it once; along the six turnings between the main views the set of front cells changes at only 14 moments, one of them at the 600-cell's own fold angle. Round one vertex the 600 cells form 15 shells, each of one kind of piece, the innermost a core of 20 Cleo-Icos filling a regular icosahedron (DICTO's piece, #19): the 600-cell's original tetrahedron as it must look in flat space. DICTO's radial cell projection unfolds the same model in 16 steps from a cell. The most graceful slice, the 48-vertex egg, is Humpty Dumpty (DICTO's name); forced to equal edges it becomes Fallen Humpty, a side note. History from Aristotle's pyramid and Kepler's nested shells; Lewis Carroll's White Queen gives the title.

Version 2 adds DICTO's observation that the fifteen Cleo shells read the same backwards (20, 20, 30, 60, 60, 60, 20, 60, 20, 60, 60, 60, 30, 20, 20), with mirrored shells' angles from the vertex adding up to exactly 180°, both from the 600-cell's symmetry through its centre.

Version 3 follows an independent review: it gives the four direction vectors and lists the exact checks run on every slice, reports Alicia Boole Stott's 1900 paper (On certain series of sections of the regular four-dimensional hypersolids), tabulates all 62 slice patterns in an appendix, and states that the study files are attached.

The ideas and names are DICTO's. Computation and proofs with Claude (Anthropic). Sources checked are listed in the paper; Alicia Boole Stott's 1900 paper, now read, is credited as the precedent: her series of the 600-cell is cell-first through the corner layers. metadata.title: The Swap Rule in Crystals: Rock Salt, Cadmium Iodide, Zinc Blende and the Laves Phases on Every Stacking
metadata.description:
Many crystals come in a cubic and a hexagonal form that differ only in how their layers are stacked, and in many mixed stackings between them. Paper #57 found that at close packing the space of every stacking is shared out into pieces borrowed from the two pure stackings, whole or in halves (the rule of halves), and #61 proved the Swap Rule: the two mixed pieces always add up to the two pure ones. Here we take both rules to four classical crystal families and prove, exactly, that the Swap Rule holds in all four, in all 299 cases where it can be tested: rock salt and nickel arsenide (NaCl, NiAs), the half-filled layers of cadmium chloride and cadmium iodide (CdCl₂, CdI₂), zinc blende and wurtzite with two different atoms (ZnS), and the Laves phases (MgCu₂, MgZn₂, MgNi₂). The rule of halves holds in full for rock salt and cadmium iodide: each octahedral piece is exactly half cubic and half hexagonal, each ball and tetrahedral piece is borrowed whole from the layer it rests on. In zinc blende the atoms keep the rule of halves, while the empty holes stop being fixed mixtures and still swap exactly. In the Laves phases, near the real alloys, every stacking is cut into exactly the same pieces.

Proof: #57's exact weight walk (rational arithmetic) on every close-packed stacking up to six layers for each family; locality checked (0 clashes); rule of halves and Swap Rule checked as exact polynomial identities in the weight. The Laves network on every stacking is built by one rule and checked against the ideal Frank–Kasper geometry.

The ideas and names are DICTO's. Computation and proof with Claude (Anthropic). Sources checked are listed in the paper. The study (scripts, raw walks, logs) is attached. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com.

metadata.title: Shadows of the Fourth Dimension: Deltahedra that Join Differently, from the Triangle-Faced Shadows and Slices of the 5-, 16-, 24- and 600-cell
metadata.description:
A deltahedron is a solid whose faces are all equilateral triangles; only eight are convex. DICTO's idea was that the three-dimensional shadows and slices of the four triangle-faced regular solids of four-dimensional space (the 5-, 16-, 24- and 600-cell) might stand closer to a new family of deltahedra than to the eight regular ones, and would join to other pieces differently. We compute every shadow and slice of the four solids along their four main directions exactly, in numbers a + b√5, and find deltahedra of two new kinds. (a) Variants that join differently: the 5-cell's edge-first shadow (TBP-5) has the pattern of the triangular bipyramid J12, and three copies of it close round an edge; the 16-cell's edge-first shadow (OCT-16) has the pattern of the octahedron, and it fills space on its own. (b) Equal-edged solids from the 600-cell: four of its shadows and slices can be rebuilt exactly with every edge equal, keeping their pattern of triangles, and all four are non-convex: a 12-dented icosahedron; the excavated and the augmented dodecahedron; Shadow-17, two diminished icosahedra (J11) glued on their pentagons, identified through DICTO's idea of cutting the pattern in halves; and Slice-48, a solid of 92 triangles with tetrahedral symmetry, found by solving the 600-cell's six large slices exactly (Singular over Q(√5), every solution found and refined to 120 digits, embedding checked with exact orientation tests). Supporting results: apart from the solids' own cells and vertex figures, no shadow, layer or slice is a regular deltahedron; bipyramids over n-gons with n ≥ 6 have no equilateral form; the other five large slices have no equilateral form with their full symmetry.

The ideas are DICTO's. Computation and proofs with Claude (Anthropic). Sources checked are listed in the paper. The study (exact arithmetic, polytopes, shadows, classification, solvers, data and logs) is attached. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com.

metadata.title: The Swap Rule: Ganesha, the Janus Tetrahedra of Squashed Stackings, and the Border at True Close Packing
metadata.description:
Stack layers of balls, cubic or hexagonal in any order, and share the space between the balls' holes by weight, as in #57 (The Rule of Halves). Here the layers are squashed or stretched. We prove that for every layer spacing from half the close-packed squash upwards (d² ≥ ⅓), in every close-packed stacking, every hole piece cut at its gap's mid-plane is the lower half of the pure piece of the layer below and the upper half of the pure piece of the layer above, tetrahedral pieces included. Consequences: the Swap Rule, V(c|h) + V(h|c) = V(c|c) + V(h|h): the two mixed pieces always add up to the two pure ones; and a sharp border at true close packing: the tetrahedral pieces are whole exactly when the layers are at least as far apart as in close packing; squashed even slightly, each mixed tetrahedral piece takes its head from one side and its body from the other. DICTO named these pieces Ganesha. Also: at close packing the three octahedral pieces end the walk in the exact ratio 4 : 5 : 6 (regular octahedron, Janus piece, rhombohedron). Proof: the substitution u = d²ζ makes every piece, its halves and the whole range of spacings and weights one convex polyhedron in five variables; 1070 exact Farkas certificates; independent exact engine check 4992 of 4992. Version 2 adds Theorem 2: below half the squash the halves stop being pure, yet every piece volume stays a sum of one share per layer type, so the Swap Rule for volumes holds for every spacing from a quarter of the squash upwards (d² ≥ 1/6), and that bound is exact (1706 further exact certificates). A map of eleven spacings shows which rule holds where; the rule was found by DICTO's idea of looking for simple rules in pictures of computed values (Splash Rules).

The ideas and names are DICTO's. Computation and proof with Claude (Anthropic). Sources checked are listed in the paper. The study (rule finder, map data, proof scripts and logs) is attached. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com.

metadata.description:

metadata.description:
In short. The pyrochlore network, small tetrahedra touching only at their corners, hides inside every diamond-like crystal: the middles of the bonds round each atom make one tetrahedron. metadata.title: The Rule of Halves: the Holes of Every Close-Packed Stacking
metadata.description:
In short. Stack layers of balls and the gaps between them are small octahedra and tetrahedra. Stack them in the cubic way (ABCABC…) or the hexagonal way (ABAB…) and these gaps are arranged differently; crystals also use countless mixed stackings, such as ABAC or ABCACB. In papers #51, #53 and #56 we slid one number, a weight, between the two kinds of gap and followed how space is shared out among them: the web of bonds. Here we follow it on every stacking at once, and find a simple rule. A tetrahedral gap always takes the piece it would have in the pure stacking of the layer it sits closest to. An octahedral gap sits half-way between two layers, and its piece is two halves: the top half is the top half of the cubic or the hexagonal piece, as the layer above decides, and the bottom half likewise from the layer below. So every stacking, of any length or pattern, is built from the two pure ones, and the kinds of piece are finite: we list them all, with exact volumes. Where a cubic layer meets a hexagonal one, octahedral pieces appear that are half cubic and half hexagonal, which DICTO calls the Janus c/h pieces ; two of them he named Chucky and Fang ; and its volume is exactly the mean of its two parents'. The proof is exact, with one bound done by hand. The rule was not found in the sources checked; its classical counterpart for the balls themselves, that each ball's surroundings are set by its own layer, is the reason the h/c notation of crystallography exists.

The ideas are DICTO's: following the web of bonds onto the other close-packed stackings (25 October 2026), and the names Chucky, Fang and Triskelion Tetrahedron, and the set name Janus c/h pieces. Computation, exact proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic); a first draft by a local open model (gpt-oss-120b) was used for the order of sections only.

metadata.title: Sonsam and Lahdeli: the Delian Bond on the Twinned Octet, with Ian Dury, Blockhead and Keyed Switch Points
metadata.description:
In short. This paper is about webs of bonds: when pieces fill space, each shared face is a bond, and the bonds together make a network that rewires as the pieces change (#52, #53). Here we follow that network on a second stacking, and show that keys change the pieces but never the network. Stack layers of balls in the cubic way (ABCABC…) and the gaps between them are octahedra and tetrahedra: the octet. Stack them in the hexagonal way (ABAB…), each layer a mirror image of its neighbours across it, and the gaps are the same octahedra and tetrahedra, joined across the mirror planes: the twinned octet. Paper #53 slid one number, a weight, between the two kinds of gap and recorded every way space splits on the way. On the cubic octet, at one exact weight, λ = 3/8 − ∛4/4 (the cube root of 2, squared: the number of the Delian problem, doubling the cube), the two pieces have equal volume: DICTO's Samson and Delilah. We follow the same walk on the twinned octet. It has its own equal-volume point, at the single root of an irreducible cubic; there the two pieces are new solids, which DICTO named Sonsam (19 corners, one face a nine-sided polygon lying on the mirror plane) and Lahdeli (12 corners), the syllables swapped as the stacking is mirrored. Further on, the twinned walk makes a stop the cubic walk does not have: Ian Dury (16 corners) with the classical 60° rhombohedron; and where the cubic walk ends in cubes the twinned one ends in Blockheads (10 corners), the twin of the cube. Every volume is exact: √2/6, 13√2/54, √2/54, √2/4. Moving a cap from one piece into its neighbour keeps the tiling and its web of bonds; done with the new pairs this gives DICTO's keyed forms Sonsam-K and Lahdeli-K, and Ian Dury-K with Rhombo-K, a six-pointed star. Finally we read DICTO's Sunstar lattice (#42) in the same light: it is rock salt's switch point (#53) keyed with Euclid's roofs. The two new walks' pieces and the keyed forms were not found in the sources checked.

The ideas are DICTO's: that further bonds may be "hiding in plain sight" in the census networks; other rhythms of volume (doubling, tripling); a different but cohesive bond network beside the golden and Delian ones; keyed versions of the new pairs; and the names Sonsam, Lahdeli, Ian Dury, Blockhead and the -K forms (25 October 2026). Computation, exact proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic).

Exact studies and checks attached (commit ca73df8). Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com.

metadata.title: One Turn Is a Gnomon: the Golden Cycle Step by Step, and the Polar of the Keyed Pair
metadata.description:
In short. Take a square of 3 × 3 dots and add an L-shaped strip of 3 + 4 dots along two sides: you get the next square, 4 × 4. The strip is a gnomon: in the classical definition (Euclid, and Heron in general), the piece which, added to a figure, makes a whole of the same shape as the figure, only larger. The gnomon method as reported for Júlia Pimentel works with exactly this strip, n + (n + 1). DICTO's idea was to carry that structure into three dimensions: walk through his golden cycle of twelve nested solids, from an icosahedron out to the next icosahedron φ³ times larger, and check at every step what it adds and whether the new whole has the shape of something before it. We built every step exactly. The answer is clean. The whole turn is a classical gnomon: the next icosahedron has the same shape as the first. No single step and no shorter run of steps is: no station has the shape of any other station, except the two icosahedra. So it is the last step, from M to the next icosahedron, that closes the gnomon. Step by step, the cycle adds spikes, pyramids, Shields and other pieces that never repeat their shapes. By volume, four steps still add a clean golden amount. DICTO's second idea concerned his keyed pair of space-filling pieces, the Lotus Jewel Axes (eight dents) and the Dodecaxes (eight keys). A dented or keyed solid has no ordinary polar, so DICTO's method is to fill the dents in (or take the keys off), take the polar of the smooth solid, and keep what was removed as the remainder. The smooth solids are the golden pair of paper #48; their polars are cubes with a low pyramid on every face, of heights 1/φ and 1/φ², which add up to exactly 1, the height that makes Kepler's rhombic dodecahedron; and the remainder is the same eight Tricaps for both pieces. Both parts read a solid by the piece that lies between it and its neighbour. Theorem A (the classical gnomon of the golden cycle). In the cycle I ⊂ Cleo star ⊂ D′ ⊂ ID ⊂ OG ⊂ rTI ⊂ TI ⊂ H ⊂ jtI ⊂ RT ⊂ M ⊂ I·φ³ the only two similar stations are I and I·φ³ (ratio φ³). Hence one whole turn, I·φ³ minus I, is a classical gnomon of I; no single step and no shorter run of steps is a classical gnomon; and, within the turn from I, the last step, M → I·φ³, is the only step whose new whole is similar to an earlier station. A polar of the Lotus Jewel Axes taken face by face about one centre would put spikes over the eight dents. All results are exact (119 checks, none failed).

metadata.title: David and Goliath: Jessen's Icosahedron and the Tetrahedron in the A15 Weight Walk
metadata.description:
In short. Paper #53 slid one number, a weight, between the two kinds of points of ten crystal arrangements and recorded, exactly, every tiling of space that appears on the way. In the A15 alloy structure (the arrangement of Cr 3 Si, and of the Weaire–Phelan foam) one stop stood out: at weight difference 3/4 the space-filling pieces are a 20-faced icosahedron around every Si point and a small tetrahedron around every Cr point. DICTO named the pair Goliath and David. Here we prove the stop exactly and identify Goliath: its corners are exactly those of Jessen's orthogonal icosahedron, so Goliath is that famous non-convex solid's convex hull. Goliath has the same shape as the classical Z12 icosahedron of A15 (Frank and Kasper), and the whole tiling is the classical picture of A15 as icosahedra and tetrahedral holes, moved by half a body diagonal; that picture is known. What we did not find in the sources searched is that the weight walk lands exactly on it, at 3/4, and the plain statement that the A15 icosahedron is Jessen's convex hull. metadata.title: The Global Web of Bonds: How Bonds Hand Over Across Crystal Networks

In short. DICTO proposed that these branches turn up elsewhere in slightly different guises. metadata.title: The Web of Bonds: How the DICTONIC Bonds Hand Over
metadata.description:
In short. DICTO's two loops of space-filling pairs, the golden loop of paper #48 and the Delian loop of paper #51, each slide one pair of solids through a whole family of shapes. Draw one line, a bond, between every two pieces that share a face, and the lines make a web. We show that each loop is really one fixed crowd of points of two kinds, the piece centres, and that the only thing that moves is one number, a weight given to one kind against the other. Every piece is the region nearer (in this weighted sense) to its own point than to any other. Then the web is exactly the web of the classical weighted Delaunay construction. As the weight slides, the bond between unlike pieces never breaks. The two like bonds hand over: in the golden loop gradually, both alive all the way and equal at Kelvin's cell; in the Delian loop all at once, at the octet, where every rhombus of a hidden rhombic dodecahedron trades its long diagonal for its short one. Read physically, the weight is a ball radius squared: the golden loop is the caesium chloride structure, the Delian loop the fluorite structure, and the range where the balls can touch is bounded exactly by Pauling's classical radius-ratio limits (the same contact condition as Pauling's).

Main theorem. For every x in [0, ∞] the golden network is the power diagram of the body-centred cubic sites with weight difference (φ²/4)(x − 1)/(x + 1); for every t in [0, 1] the Delian network is the power diagram of the fluorite sites with weight difference (3/8)(2t − 1). The web is the 1-skeleton of the dual regular subdivision, with exact bond areas. At the ends, at Kelvin's cell and at the octet these are classical Voronoi or Delaunay tessellations; the theorem gives the whole family between them. In the golden loop all three bond types live on the whole open loop, with constant face lattice; the two like bonds have area ratio x² and are equal only at x = 1. In the Delian loop the unlike bond lives exactly on (0, 1), oct–oct exactly on [0, 1/3), tet–tet exactly on (1/3, 1]; t = 1/3, the octet, is the only parameter at which both pieces exist and only one bond type is present.

Theorem 2 (the balls): the weight is a squared radius; with unlike neighbours touching, ρ = (x + 2)/(2x + 1) and ρ = t/(1 − t), and the touching windows end exactly at Pauling's limits √3 − 1 and √(3/2) − 1 (Pauling's own contact condition, rederived). All geometric results are exact (371 + 61 checks, none failed; the 24 physical checks of the scale-anomaly study are estimates).

The ideas are DICTO's: the DICTONIC SOLIDS and the DICTONIC BONDS and their names, and the web of bonds, a network of bonds that "should create a web of lattices that change with the rhythm of the loop" (DICTO, 25 October 2026); computation, exact proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). More at dictospheres.com.

metadata.title: One Move Each: Classical Cut-and-Glue Space-Fillers Built Exactly
metadata.description:
In short. Books describe several classical solids that fill space by how to make them from other solids: shave a belt off one, stick two pyramids onto another, glue a few slanted bricks together. Kaleidohedra makes the same solids in one go, by tilting and stretching a lattice of points, and so gives every corner and every volume exactly. The moves themselves are Fedorov's (1885); what this paper adds is the exact data, the settings and the proofs.

Main theorem. Five space-fillers that the literature gives by cutting, gluing, zone removal or a drawing are each obtained exactly by one setting of Kaleidohedra's three moves: a shear of the lattice, the equal-edged cell (Cell = 1) and a stretch along a free direction. With edge 1: the regular-hexagon elongated dodecahedron, volume 4√2, symmetry D2h; the Bain rhombic dodecahedron, 2√2, D4h; the classical elongated dodecahedron, 8/3 + 16√3/9, D4h; the Bilinski dodecahedron, (4/5)√(5 + 2√5), D2h; and the 60° rhombohedron, 1/√2, D3d. Each tiles space by translation and is congruent, corner by corner, to its classical construction. Theorem 2: every rhombic-dodecahedron-type cell has exactly three free directions. The Bilinski dodecahedron is glued exactly from two acute and two obtuse golden rhombohedra, and DICTO's skewed rhombic dodecahedron (F1) is a linear image of it.

The idea, that Kaleidohedra's lattice moves rebuild exactly the space-fillers the literature gives by cutting and gluing, is DICTO's, as are his skewed rhombic dodecahedron (F1) and his route to the regular-hexagon elongated dodecahedron (F5); computation, proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). More at dictospheres.com.

metadata.title: The Delian Bond: Samson, Delilah and the Octet Between Kepler's Rhombic Dodecahedron and the Cube
metadata.description:
In short. Regular tetrahedra and octahedra fill space together: the octet. Join each tetrahedron's centre to each octahedron's centre through the face they share, cut every such double cone by one flat plane parallel to that face, and give each side to its own centre. Slide the cut, and every position still fills space with two convex solids, from Kepler's rhombic dodecahedra through the octet to cubes. At one position the two solids have exactly the same volume: the tetrahedron's piece has doubled and the octahedron's halved, the doubling of the ancient Delian problem in both directions at once. DICTO named this pair Samson and Delilah.

Main theorem. For every cut position t from 0 to 1 the two pieces are convex and fill space face to face: for t ≤ 1/3 a regular tetrahedron of edge 3t and a rhombic dodecahedron with its eight three-fold corners cut, for t ≥ 1/3 a regular octahedron of edge 3(1 − t)/2 and a cube with four alternate corners cut, with exact volumes. Theorem 2: at t = (2√6 − 3)/15 and t = 5/3 − (2/3)√2 every edge is equal; at t = 1 − ∛6/3 the two kinds each fill half of space. Theorem 3 (the Delian bond): at t = 1 − (2/3)·2−1/3, and only there, the two pieces have equal volume: Samson, the cut cube, twice the octet's tetrahedron, and Delilah, a regular octahedron, half the octet's octahedron. Exact in ℚ(√6), ℚ(√2), ℚ(∛2) and ℚ(∛6).

With paper #48 this gives DICTO's six DICTONIC SOLIDS in three DICTONIC BONDS (golden, keyed, Delian). Not all six are new as shapes; what is new is each bond. A remark shows that the same weighted cut for the cube meets only known solids (truncated cubic, rectified cubic and Kelvin's honeycombs), so the count stays at three bonds; another remark gives the polar pair of #48. The family through the octet, its equal-edged and half-and-half members and the Delian bond were not found in the sources checked.

The ideas, and the names Samson, Delilah, DICTONIC SOLIDS and DICTONIC BONDS, are DICTO's; computation, exact proofs and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). More at dictospheres.com.

metadata.title: The Golden Split: Icosahedra, Unborns and AXE Become Two Convex Space-Fillers
metadata.description:
In short. Icosahedra cannot fill space on their own. Set them in a cubic grid, edge to edge, and two kinds of gap are left: a squeezed icosahedron (the Unborn) in the middle of each cube, and thin tetrahedra (the AXE) between them. Cut each AXE into four pyramids from the point 1/φ of the way along its axis and give each pyramid to the piece it touches: the icosahedra and the Unborns become two convex truncated octahedra that fill space.

Main theorem. In the simple cubic lattice of regular icosahedra of edge 1 and spacing φ, the golden split of every AXE makes the icosahedron with its 12 pyramids, the Icosaxes, and the Unborn with its 12, the Unborn Axes, convex truncated octahedra with full octahedral symmetry, the same equiangular hexagon (sides 1/√2 and 1/(φ√2)), volumes 1 + 2√5/3 and 1 + √5/3, filling space face to face. Theorem 2: for any cut points inside the AXEs, both padded pieces are convex only if every AXE is cut at its golden point. Theorem 3: in the Lotus Jewel network the same cut gives the keyed pair Lotus Jewel Axes (volume √5) and Dodecaxes (volume 2), and every keying fills space. Theorem 4 (factor x): the pair belongs to a one-parameter family of mixed space-fillers, the truncated octahedra T(x) and T(1/x), from Kelvin's cell (x = 1) to the golden pair (x = τ). A remark places the octet (tetrahedra and octahedra) in a similar family between the rhombic dodecahedron and the cube. Exact in ℚ(√5). The two smooth shapes are known (Koca et al. 2015, x = τ and x = 1/τ); the route from the icosahedron lattice, the golden split and its uniqueness, and the keyed pair were not found in the sources checked.

Paper #48 continues DICTO's search for mixed Platonic space-fillers (#47), answering his conjecture that a more elegant and simpler filling was within reach. metadata.title: The DICTO Ogdoecontahedron on the Octet Truss
metadata.description:
Joined hexagon to hexagon, copies of the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron (OG) form a body-centred cubic packing whose gap is treated in a companion paper (DICTO DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23451210). Here the OG goes the other way: its eight joint hexagons lie exactly on the faces of a regular octahedron |x| + |y| + |z| = 2φ/3, so the OG sits in the octahedra of the octet truss, and the space round it becomes tractable. Exactly, in ℚ(√5), we give four families of space-filling kits. (1) A golden-key octet: the OG's golden envelope (a rhombic triacontahedron) pokes into each neighbouring tetrahedron as a small key whose base corners sit at the golden-section points of the octahedron's edges; keyed octahedron and dented tetrahedron (a left and a right) fill space. (2) A Penrose-core octet: the five-fold stars of neighbouring OGs face each other across every octahedron edge, offset by exactly one star tip radius, and an exact thick Penrose rhombus, with two φ-smaller ones, joins them; the shared middle piece holds three Penrose cores. (3) Golden envelopes on every octahedron never overlap and fill exactly 90 − 40√5 = 10/φ⁶ ≈ 55.73% of space; the rest is one chiral piece, so envelope and grown piece fill space with two shapes, and each envelope lies inside its rhombic dodecahedron touching all 12 faces at golden-section points. (4) One-piece glue: the rhombic dodecahedron round each octet vertex, or the octahedral cell round each edge midpoint, minus the OGs that bite it, fills space with the OG as two shapes with no mirror pair, the sockets being exact OG imprints; the edge-centred piece holds all three Penrose cores and can be keyed with the OG's own kites so that twelve copies lock round one OG. The main kits were proved exactly by an independent engine and checked with millions of sample points.

Ideas, choices and names are DICTO's; computation, exact arithmetic and renders were done with Claude (Anthropic) as a research assistant; the independent exact proofs, the vertex glue W, the identification of the tetartoid and the keyed-glue design are by Claude Fable. metadata.title: The Polyhedral Stretching Theorem
metadata.description:
In short. Take a regular dodecahedron and slide it one edge-length in a straight line. The shape it sweeps through has every edge the same length, whichever way you slide it, except when the slide runs exactly along one of its edges.

Main theorem (the Polyhedral Stretching Theorem). Let P be a convex polyhedron whose edges all have length 1, and slide it a distance 1 along a direction u. The swept shape (the convex hull of P and P moved by u) has every edge of length 1 unless u is parallel to an edge of P. Its faces are: each face of P not parallel to u, kept whole; each n-sided face parallel to u, stretched into an (n+2)-gon, with one side fewer for each of its edges parallel to u; and one parallelogram for every edge of P's outline seen along u, a rhombus when the slide is 1. The proof is given in an appendix.

For the dodecahedron: sliding along a cube axis gives DICTO's stretched dodecahedron (F11); along a five-fold axis the ten rhombi are all alike; along a face diagonal of Euclid's cube it gives the member DICTO found, all twelve pentagons and ten rhombi, which began as a void and two overlapping dodecahedra that DICTO saw in the dodecahedron layer of paper #47. Dodecahedra at the corners of a triangle or a tetrahedron give three- and four-cap forms with equilateral triangles among their faces. The theorem holds for every Platonic solid: the stretched icosahedra form a second new-looking family, and the tetrahedron and octahedron rediscover the cuboctahedron, the truncated tetrahedron and three Johnson solids. DICTO names the family the DICTO stretched solids: equal-edged when the stretch is one edge-length, telescoped at any other length.

metadata.title: Every Mix of the Platonic Solids Fills Space
metadata.description:
Main theorem. metadata.title: Aristotle's Pyramid
metadata.description:
Main theorem. Of the five face pyramids of the Platonic solids (the cone from the centre over one face), a set fills space exactly when it is the cube's pyramid alone, the tetrahedron's and the octahedron's pyramids together, or the union of these two; no other set fills space. Here a set fills space when copies of its pyramids, in any numbers, any positions and mirror images, every kind used and not necessarily face to face, tile space. The proof is a Dehn-type counting map on dihedral angles, made rigorous with the Splitting Theorem of Conway, Radin and Sadun: the dodecahedron's and the icosahedron's pyramids can never occur, and the tetrahedron's occurs exactly when the octahedron's does; the octet truss cut from its centres and the cubic tiling give the tilings. Corollaries: alone only the cube's pyramid fills space, in pairs only the tetrahedron's with the octahedron's, and with equal edges their numbers are asymptotically equal; the icosahedron's pyramid, the Cleo-Icos (DICTO's name), fills space only with a partner that is not a face pyramid, Antonius (#20). The question is DICTO's: Aristotle wrote that among solids only "the pyramid and the cube" fill space (On the Heavens III.8); read as the regular tetrahedron this is false, and DICTO asked whether he could have meant the Cleo-Icos. A section after the theorem collects DICTO's earlier exact fillings by the whole Platonic solids with partners. Every angle identity, the test over all 31 sets and the constructions are checked in exact arithmetic.

metadata.title: The Reuleaux Platonic Solids
metadata.description:
Main theorem. Put a ball on every corner of a Platonic solid of diameter 1, each of radius 1, and let B be what all the balls share (DICTO's idea). Then the smallest width of B is exactly 1, reached along any line through two corners at distance 1; and for the cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron, with circumradius ½ and inradius r, the width along each axis through a face centre is exactly 2√(3/4 + r²) − 2r. Corollary: dual solids have the same ratio r/R, so dual pairs have exactly the same face-axis width, (√30 − √3)/3 ≈ 1.248392 for the balls on the cube and on the octahedron and (√(50 + 2√5) − √(5 + 2√5))/√15 ≈ 1.110989 for the balls on the dodecahedron and on the icosahedron. The tetrahedron is the classical case, the Reuleaux tetrahedron, where the formula does not apply (its diameter is its edge, not twice its circumradius); its edge-midpoint axis gives √3 − √2/2 by the same argument, and our volume agrees with the known closed form to 1.1 × 10−8. The four other bodies (not found in the sources checked) are not Reuleaux polyhedra in the sense of Montejano and Roldán-Pensado, following Sallee, or of Hynd. Conjecture 1, with numerical evidence from 3000 directions and local refinement: these axes give the largest width. DICTO names the bodies by their look, the Reuleaux octahedron (balls on the cube), cube (on the octahedron), icosahedron (on the dodecahedron) and dodecahedron (on the icosahedron); each has the face pattern of the dual solid, and the fewest face colours are 4, 2, 3, 3 and 4.

metadata.description:
Regular dodecahedra on alternate cubes of a cubic lattice (Euclid's dodecahedron: a cube with a roof on each face) are the densest lattice packing of the dodecahedron [9]; the hole left in each other cube is a star, the Dogstar, and dodecahedra and Dogstars fill space. metadata.description:

metadata.title: The DICTO Ogdoecontahedron on the Gyrated Octet
metadata.description:
In a companion paper the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron (OG) sits in every octahedron of the octet truss, its eight joint hexagons on the eight faces. DICTO proposed that it can also live in the gyrated octet, the tetrahedral–octahedral honeycomb stacked A B A B, in which octahedron meets octahedron and tetrahedron meets tetrahedron across every layer. It can: the OGs on both sides of a layer meet on the same joint hexagon, but each is the mirror image of the other, and since the OG has no such mirror the layers are twin boundaries; exactly, the twin is the OG turned 60° about the joint three-fold axis, the spinel law of crystallography. Cutting each octahedron into the OG and eight chiral caps, and keeping the tetrahedra whole, gives one exact kit for the octet, the gyrated octet and every stacking between; at a twin layer a left and a right cap join into a twin cap and two tetrahedra into a triangular bipyramid. The facing-star middle piece of the octet fails at twin layers, and a mirror middle piece of volume (424 − 88√5)/4617 takes its place; with one boundary cap and one boundary tetrahedron the octet's Penrose-core kit then fills the gyrated octet and a single twin layer exactly, and with the same pieces any stacking; its Penrose cores lie only on the edges within the layers. The trait runs in the family: the OCD Stella twins in the same way, meeting its twin on a whole joint triangle; the golden envelope does not fit as it is, but cut flat at two opposite three-fold corners it becomes a solid of its own, the DICTO Belted Triacontahedron (DBT), which fills the gyrated octet's octahedra pole to pole without overlap, 55.02% of space. Cut the same way at all eight of the corners that point through the octahedron's faces, it becomes the DICTO Octahedrally Truncated Triacontahedron (DICTO OTT), with the OG's own symmetry, which twins like the OG, lies inside its octahedron and so fits every stacking, 52.89% of space. For each, the rest of space is filled by one more shape (two hands of one in the octet): the DICTO Fill sets. The DICTO Jewel's packing, framed by cubes, does not continue across a twin layer. All claims are exact in ℚ(√5) except where marked float.

metadata.title: The DICTO OG Family on Every Stacking
metadata.description:
One exact kit of pieces builds the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron (OG) into the octet, the gyrated octet, the classical polytypes between them and a Fibonacci crystal that never repeats; the OG family stacks like a real mineral, twinning by the spinel law. Two short rules say why. The tetrahedral–octahedral honeycomb falls into layers, and each layer can be laid on the one below in two ways: as in the octet truss (c) or as its mirror image in the shared plane (h). Any word in c and h is a stacking, exactly as for close-packed crystals, whose polytypes 3C, 2H, 4H, 6H, 9R, 15R … are words of this kind. The OG sits exactly in the octahedra of the octet [2] and of the gyrated octet [3]; here we place it, and the solids of its family, in every stacking. The twin rule: if a solid is centrosymmetric and has a three-fold axis at right angles to the layers, its mirror image in a layer plane is the same solid turned 60° about that axis; unless it also has a mirror at right angles to the axis, this is a true twin. The fit rule: a solid that lies in its own layer and does not overlap its copies within the layer fits every stacking, whatever the word. The OG, the DICTO OTT and the OCD Stella lie in their octahedra, and [3] showed that they fit every stacking; the rules explain why. The DICTO Belted Triacontahedron (DBT) leaves its octahedron but not its layer, so it too fits every stacking (shown in [3] only for the gyrated octet); exactly in ℚ(√5), the golden envelope (a rhombic triacontahedron) it was cut from fits the octet but overlaps at every h plane by exactly the volume of the two tips the DBT removes. The shares of space do not depend on the stacking: OG 1025/114 − 145√5/38 ≈ 45.89%, OTT 176/3 − 26√5 ≈ 52.89%, DBT 493/6 − 73√5/2 ≈ 55.02%. For the OG we give the kit per cell for 3C, 2H, 4H, 6H, 9R and 15R, and for the Fibonacci stacking (c → ch, h → c), which never repeats: in the limit exactly (3 − √5)/2 of the planes between layers are h planes (twin planes), and a cell needs 5 + √5 caps, (3 − √5)/2 twin caps, √5 − 1 tetrahedra and (3 − √5)/2 bipyramids, all exact.

metadata.title: Universal PiTet: The DICTO PiTet Proposition
metadata.description:
DICTO specified a five-fold version of the octet: spherical shells grown outward from the Cleo star, the same pattern each time with different solids, triangles and pyramids staying constant (hence the name PiTet: Pi for the spherical progression, Tet for the triangles). We give a rule that does this and prove, in exact arithmetic in ℚ(√5), what it produces. Let T take a convex solid with corners v to the solid {x : v·x ≤ v·v for every corner v}: each new face passes through a corner of the last solid at right angles to it. Starting from the icosidodecahedron (ID), T gives the rhombic triacontahedron (RT), then the DICTO GTI (Golden Truncated Icosahedron: hexagon sides 1 : φ), then the DICTO FPD (Flat Pentakis Dodecahedron), and then the ID again, exactly 10/φ⁴ = 35 − 15√5 times larger; the cycle therefore repeats without end. Each solid lies in the next, each shell is filled by congruent pieces of one or two kinds (exact volumes), and the whole chain is its own polar about the GTI's circumsphere. Below the cycle, the Cleo star (82 pieces) and 12 twisted frusta (Monkey Staff B) close the ID; the pieces on one five-fold axis join into a convex five-sided Vajra, and the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron fits between the ID and the RT with 20 pure hexagonal Cleos. metadata.description:
In Universal PiTet a single rule T builds each solid from the last: every corner v of a solid S gives the face plane v·x = v·v, through v and at right angles to the line from the centre, and T(S) is the solid these planes bound. Started at the icosidodecahedron it closes into a four-step cycle. DICTO proposed running it from the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron (OG), and also running it the other way. The reverse step P takes as new corners the foot points of S's face planes, the points of those planes nearest the centre. From the OG, four steps of T give four solids with 92, 180, 212 and 270 corners, the DICTO KRE, PHE, TPP and DPHP, and four steps of P give four with 80, 132, 140 and 162 corners, the DICTO TPH, TQH, TQP and TQHD. All eight are proved exactly in ℚ(√5), each with the full icosahedral symmetry, and each step of P is undone exactly by T. Several have regular faces: 12 regular pentagons (PHE, TPH, TQP), 20 regular hexagons (PHE, DPHP, TQH, TQHD); the KRE has 30 rhombi and 60 kites. The family does not cycle. It nests as shells for three steps up, OG ⊂ KRE ⊂ PHE ⊂ TPP, and two steps down, TQH ⊂ TPH ⊂ OG, and each of these shells, and also the shell TQHD ⊂ TQP, is filled exactly by one piece per face of the inner solid. Both directions then break in the same way: 60 corners of the TPP stand outside the DPHP, and 60 corners of the TQP outside the TQH. In the plane, T and P are the classical antipedal and pedal constructions; the polyhedral pedal construction was posed as an open problem in 2010. We found the eight solids in no source.

metadata.title: A Fibonacci Spine in a Five-fold Chorus of Ogdoecontahedron Packings
metadata.description:
The DICTO Ogdoecontahedron is a convex, centrally symmetric icosahedral solid with 20 regular hexagons and 60 kites. Its hexagon directions contain five inscribed cubes, and each cube gives a periodic (body-centred cubic) packing in which copies meet face to face on hexagons. We place the five packings ("voices") in five 72° wedges round a five-fold axis, which is the icosahedral irrational twin, and remove clashing copies in whole five-fold rings. Checked exactly in ℚ(√5), the result is overlap-free to radius 10 (2756 sites, 385 removed, 7465 close pairs). Every copy lies at a golden height (m + nφ)u along the axis. Apart from one ring, the removed copies nearest the axis lie in one plane on a rank-2 lattice with axis slope −φ; together with the central copy, which is kept, they are exactly the points of the canonical singular Fibonacci cut-and-project chain with window [0, W), W² = 64/81 + 128√5/405. The window has a mechanism: a ring of five plane copies overlaps itself exactly when it is closer to the axis than tc, tc² = 8/9 + 8√5/45. Since tc < W and no plane lattice point lies between them for |h| < 12.81, the two windows select the same points there. At h = 12.81 the core copy overlaps one other copy, which overlaps two more; on finite patches (integer program, float clash test) keeping the core copy is cheaper by one ring, here and at the next three such points. Minimal removal therefore thins the spine to a three-gap chain beyond |h| = 12.81, and staying pure Fibonacci costs at least one extra ring at each such point. Thus aperiodic order appears where periodic packings meet: the lattice of the chain is a plane section of one packing, its internal coordinate is the distance from the axis, and its window is fixed by the ring clash at tc. Irrational interfaces as one-dimensional quasicrystals, model sets near irrational lines and hard-core windows are known; we did not find this selection along a five-fold junction line, its self-clash window or the departure from it, and present them as a new exact instance of known ideas.

metadata.description:
We hollow the DICTO-ICOSA star (the DICTO-Star with a pyramid on each of its 152 free faces) and find that a core icosahedron resting on twelve inner tips is loose: it turns about 14° before it touches anything. Their points land exactly on the face centres of an icosahedron of edge 1, the same edge as every other piece, because the icosidodecahedron's triangles lie at twice that icosahedron's inradius; held so, the core cannot turn or shift. In the stations (215 pieces) every layer is a closed solid, each Cleo-Ico fused with the dodecahedron's corner pyramid into an Atraktos. metadata.title: The DICTO Ogdoecontahedron
metadata.description:
DICTO proposed turning the Spheres of Dharma, an exact endless nesting of six icosahedral solids, inside out. We include the cycle's in-between stage, the DICTO Truncated-Icosahedral Hecatodihedron, as a seventh station and take every station's polar reciprocal: the nesting reverses, and every station becomes a classical solid except one. The polar of the Hecatodihedron is new, and DICTO named it the Ogdoecontahedron for its 80 faces. It has 20 regular hexagons and 60 kites, 102 corners and 180 edges, only two edge lengths and two dihedral angles, no insphere and no midsphere, and 90 of its corners on one sphere, the inside-out image of the Hecatodihedron's 90 faces touching one sphere; every coordinate is exact in ℚ(√5). It is the pentakis dodecahedron with its 20 six-fold corners cut off flat. In the reversed cycle its 90 sphere corners lie on the icosidodecahedron's sphere, its hexagons hold the icosidodecahedron's triangles and its kites lie in the pentakis dodecahedron's faces. Its face arrangement is known (the dual of L0 applied to the dodecahedron, in the notation of the Antiprism software), but the metric solid was not found in the sources checked. Copies joined face to face on hexagons form a diamond network whose joints lie on a pyrochlore lattice; two such networks together are a body-centred cubic packing filling exactly (9225 − 3915√5)/608 ≈ 77.43% of space. It is neither a patch nor a cluster of the canonical (primitive) icosahedral quasicrystal; five of its periodic packings meeting round a five-fold axis are the subject of a separate paper (#30).

metadata.title: Golden Bodhi Pyrochlore
metadata.description:
Copies of the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron joined face to face on their hexagons form a body-centred cubic packing that fills (9225 − 3915√5)/608 ≈ 77.43% of space (DICTO DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23404688). This paper is about the remaining 22.57%. Exactly, in ℚ(√5): each copy's share of the gap is its Voronoi cell, a truncated octahedron, minus the solid, and cones from the centre over the 72 free faces cut it into 72 convex pieces of 3 kinds whose volumes add up with remainder 0. Asking what could fill the gap more naturally, DICTO proposed partners, bridges, hexagonal limbs and adapters. The limbs are tilted hexagonal prisms, one per free hexagon, which cross in pairs at the centres of the cell's square faces; their crossing zone has exactly two golden-rhombus faces, the faces of the rhombic triacontahedron and the golden rhombohedra. From there a golden fill suggests itself: golden rhombohedra, DICTO's Cleo-Icos as adapters from hexagons to golden planes, and the Bodhi pieces, which are all bounded by golden-rhombus planes. Each copy's golden envelope is a rhombic triacontahedron; cut at the joints, the envelopes divide the packing into 77.4% solid, 11.8% non-golden shell and 10.7% golden region. But the golden region does not divide naturally into Bodhi pieces: cut canonically by every golden plane, even in DICTO's five-fold chorus arrangement, it shatters into 8,027 pieces (exact), with only five Bodhi pieces among them. So we ask what any golden fill must contain. Exactly: the golden region's walls are golden planes except for 24 small star-tip triangles per cell, which lie in the three-fold joint planes and meet the neighbouring golden faces at 20.905° (cos² = φ²/3), so golden rhombohedra and Bodhi pieces alone can never fill it. One adapter removes the obstruction: the GBPC (Golden Bodhi Pyrochlore Corner), a low triangular pyramid shaped like the rhombic triacontahedron's three-fold corner and the golden conjugate of DICTO's Cleo-Ico, 24 per cell, overlapping nothing. What remains has only golden walls and five-fold edges, and no local obstruction is left. But it has no face-to-face tiling by golden rhombohedra: for one size, its walls fix the edge at a rational multiple of φ and a Galois-conjugate count then demands a negative number of oblate rhombohedra (exact; the counting step checked independently); and a face-to-face tiling cannot mix sizes. Whether it tiles other than face to face is open; random and symmetric searches fill at most 66.9% of it, and flat slabs between second neighbours need golden layers of sizes our searches did not use. DICTO's own answer to the gap is not golden but whole: cut point by point at the octahedral holes of the bcc lattice, three per copy, each between six copies, the gap falls into identical pieces, the Bull-horns OG adaptor, partly golden-faced, each exactly one third of a copy's gap, (18728 − 6296√5)/41553 ≈ 0.111898 or 7.5223% of space; copies and adaptors fill space exactly with two shapes. Float explorations are labelled as such.

metadata.title: Inverted Shells: The Spheres of Dharma Turned Inside Out
metadata.description:
The Spheres of Dharma nest six icosahedral solids exactly, from an icosahedron out to the icosahedron φ³ larger; between the truncated icosahedron and the triacontahedron, the layer closes part-way into the DICTO Hecatodihedron. DICTO proposed turning the cycle inside out. Turning each layer's pieces over does not work: no layer closes into a shell. Taking the six solids and the Hecatodihedron stage as seven stations and replacing each by its polar reciprocal reverses the nesting and gives a new exact cycle: dodecahedron ⊂ icosidodecahedron ⊂ Ogdoecontahedron ⊂ pentakis dodecahedron ⊂ icosahedron ⊂ rhombic triacontahedron ⊂ dodecahedron φ³ larger (volume ratio φ⁹). The cycle inherits two loose ends. Tightening them gives an evenly stepped nest, still one kind per layer and exact. Left loose, the large outer gap holds the great stellated dodecahedron at exactly one size: its 20 points on the outer dodecahedron's corners, its 12 valleys on the triacontahedron's tips, cutting the gap into 60 tetrahedra and 60 pentagonal pyramids. The inner gap admits no star and no locked dual pair among those tested, but the truncated icosidodecahedron pair fits in reverse order (as polarity demands), with play exactly √5·φ³/9. The golden rectangles that frame the whole are the outer dodecahedron's own small stellation, and the cycle repeats inward without end. metadata.title: The FUJI Family: Pyramids on Flat-Ended Triangles
metadata.description:
FUJI is the hexagonal pyramid that closes the corners of our thirteen-icosahedron cluster, the Lotus seed [1]. Its base is a flat-ended triangle: a hexagon with all angles 120° and sides 1 and 1/φ alternating. The same shape kept turning up elsewhere, in our cuboctahedral PET-bottle spheres and in the colouring of the Lotus seed, so we asked whether FUJI belongs to a family.

It does. Put an apex over a flat-ended triangle with sides 1 and r, with all six side edges of length 1. This gives a one-parameter family FUJI(r), running from the regular tetrahedron (r = 0) through FUJI (r = 1/φ) to the flat regular hexagon (r = 1). We derive the base angles and prove:

  • The base angles (derived): cos L = (1 + 2r)/3 and cos² S = (2 + r)/(3(2 − r)).
  • The antiprism rule: the member whose base continues the plane of the n-gonal antiprism's triangles is r = 2 cos(π/n) − 1, so that 1 + r is the short diagonal of the regular n-gon (for n = 3, its side).
  • The wheel bound: flat wheels crossing along different spokes number at most 3 (square), 4 (hexagonal) or 6 (decagonal), and five octagonal wheels are impossible. The octahedron gives the tetrahedron, the square antiprism √2 − 1, and the pentagonal antiprism (the middle of the icosahedron) gives FUJI.

The members turn up in several places:

  • The golden hexagon of a construction after Odom is FUJI's base; the same construction with any extension gives every member with r < 1.
  • The space-filling truncated tetrahedron of Damasceno, Engel and Glotzer has the r = 1/2 member's base as its faces.
  • In a breathing pyrochlore the kagome hexagons are flat-ended triangles, with r equal to the breathing ratio; as a Wythoff construction it tiles space for every r.
  • The equal-depth cube–octahedron solid has the cuboctahedral member's base, r = (√3 − 1)/2, as its eight triangles, and its cube corners are exactly that member's apexes; we prove the two conditions are the same.
  • Cleo-Icos and Antonius: the icosahedron's central pyramid is the corner of the prolate golden rhombohedron, which splits into Cleo-Icos + Antonius + Cleo-Icos; so the two fill space, two to one, and build the rhombic hexecontahedron.

DICTO · dictospheres.com. Computation, checking and drafting with Claude (Anthropic). Data, scripts, proofs and checks: studies/2026-10-14-fuji-family in https://github.com/DICTOR-Master/kaleidohedra.

Version 3 credits the Cleo-Icos as the unit tetrahedron of the Mackay icosahedron (Mackay 1962; Ino 1969; Marks 1984; Kabai 2014) and the golden rhombohedron as a distorted fcc cell (Prodan et al. 2017).

Version 4 (2026-10-14): the Cleo-Icos in classical geometry, as the twin of the dodecahedron's central pyramid in Hypsicles' "Book XIV" of Euclid (c. 150 BC); the golden-hexagon construction credited to Sándor Kabai's Wolfram Demonstration "Hexagons and the Golden Ratio" (2008). No other changes.

metadata.description:
We describe a convex polyhedron with 102 faces, 80 corners and 180 edges that arises as the seventh stage of our Spheres of Dharma, a cycle of nested icosahedral shells. It is the truncated icosahedron with a low hexagonal pyramid (a Shield) on each of its 20 hexagons, at the one height at which the two triangles of neighbouring Shields across every hexagon–hexagon edge lie in a single plane. Its faces are 12 regular pentagons, 30 rhombi and 60 isosceles triangles; it has only two edge angles. Combinatorially it is Conway's hexakis truncated icosahedron k6tI (132 faces) with its 60 coplanar triangle pairs merged into 30 rhombi. The rhombi and triangles all touch one sphere; the pentagons lie a little inside it, so the solid has no insphere. We name it the DICTO Truncated-Icosahedral Hecatodihedron (hecatodi-, one hundred and two). This corrects an earlier statement of ours that all 102 faces touch one sphere.

metadata.title: DICTO ATOM-13×13: thirteen clusters of thirteen, twelve around one, six golden and seven periodic, with the pieces that fill between them
metadata.description:
Twelve equal spheres can touch a thirteenth and no more (Schütte and van der Waerden 1952), and twelve atoms round one make the icosahedral cluster of liquids and metals (Frank 1952). We set thirteen polyhedral thirteens side by side, each a centre and twelve around it. Six are golden, on the icosahedron's five-fold axes: the Icosa-13 (Lotus seed), DESHI, the Dodeca-13, UNITY with its closed form VENUS, the DICTO-Star and the Bodhi seed. Seven are periodic, a cell and twelve neighbours in a honeycomb: the rhombic dodecahedron (RD 13, with its rounded form the DICTO Spheroid-13 RD), our skewed RD, the Bain RD, the golden Bilinski dodecahedron, the regular-hexagon elongated dodecahedron, the truncated octahedron (4 + 5 + 4, the centre seen through two square windows) and the DICTO Jewel (with its stella octangulas). For each we give how the twelve touch the centre and one another, and the kits that fill between them: 24 kits from 13 to 213 pieces, every one checked piece by piece and buildable from the centre out. Two golden clusters close exactly into a φ²-times larger copy of their own form. Every periodic block fills space by translation alone, and all seven are the same tiling in different shapes: under a linear change of coordinates each neighbourhood is the face-centred cubic one, whose radius-one perfect code is known (Kovačević and Tan 2018; explicitly x₁ + 3x₂ + 9x₃ ≡ 0 mod 13, Kovačević 2026), its weights Singer's difference set {0, 1, 3, 9} mod 13 (Singer 1938).

metadata.title: DICTO Spheroid-13 RD: a true rhombic dodecahedron wrapped by twelve keyed pieces, a nearly round block of thirteen that fills space by translation alone
metadata.description:
A rhombic dodecahedron with its twelve face neighbours, thirteen cells of the face-centred cubic (FCC) honeycomb, fills space by translation alone: of the 183 sublattices of index 13 in the FCC lattice, exactly 8 have the thirteen lattice points as a complete set of representatives, and the 8 are turns of one arrangement, with block translations of length √10 (neighbour spacing √2). Keeping that tiling, we reshape the block: the centre stays a true rhombic dodecahedron, only larger, and the twelve cells around it are moved, corner class by corner class and the same in every block, with every face flat and every cell convex with a minimum thickness, to make the block's outer surface as small as possible. The result, the DICTO Spheroid-13 RD, is nearly round while its outside stays keyed: at minimum thickness 0.15 its roundness 36πV²/S³ is 0.707 (the plain block 0.365, a single rhombic dodecahedron 0.741, and the block lattice's Voronoi cell, the roundest single tile with these translations, 0.748), with a centre 1.525 times the size of the lattice's own cells. The block has the tiling's full symmetry (order 6), so it uses three piece shapes: the centre and two outer kinds of six, each three pieces and their mirror images. Each block meets 14 others across all 84 of its outer faces; the centres never meet. Four thicknesses are given (0.08 to 0.35), with printable nets at one scale per set; as a variant, the centre left free to reshape gains at most 0.01 in roundness. The block tiling itself is known: it is the radius-one perfect code of the A₃ lattice (Kovačević and Tan 2018), written explicitly as x₁ + 3x₂ + 9x₃ ≡ 0 (mod 13) by Kovačević (2026), and its weights 0, 1, 3, 9 are Singer's perfect difference set of the projective plane of order 3. What is new here is the block as thirteen rhombic dodecahedra, rounded and keyed around a true rhombic dodecahedron, with its pieces and nets.

Credit: the question whether the rhombic dodecahedron's thirteen fills space as the DICTO Hexa does, the rounded, keyed quality of the block, the true rhombic dodecahedron at its centre, the choice of thicknesses and the name DICTO Spheroid-13 RD are DICTO's. metadata.title: Spheres of Dharma: a second endless golden cycle of the icosahedral solids, through the icosidodecahedron, the fullerene cage and the rhombic triacontahedron
metadata.description:
We describe an exact, endlessly repeating nesting of six icosahedral solids (the Ritsudō cycle), each layer filled by a few repeated pieces. With the dodecahedron at edge 1: an icosahedron of edge 1/φ, an icosidodecahedron of edge φ/2 (around it 12 pentagonal pyramids and 20 twisted triangular frusta), the dodecahedron (20 triangular pyramids), a truncated icosahedron of edge 1/φ, the fullerene cage (12 twisted pentagonal frusta and 30 Mosseri–Sadoc tetrahedra t1 at scale 1/φ), a rhombic triacontahedron of edge ½√(45 − 18√5) = 1.089814 (12 pentagonal and 20 hexagonal caps and 60 tetrahedral wedges), and an icosahedron of edge φ² (30 edge and 20 face pieces). The outer icosahedron is φ³ times the inner one, so the cycle repeats without end in both directions; one cycle has 237 pieces. All pieces of a cycle are checked to be free of overlap, with total volume exact. The construction rests on three exact relations: the icosahedron and the dodecahedron share the icosidodecahedron as their core, differing only in 12 pentagonal or 20 triangular corner pyramids; the fullerene cage wraps the dodecahedron at exactly one golden step, the dodecahedron's corners on the cage's hexagon centres; and the rhombic triacontahedron is the cage, with its 60 corners on the triacontahedron's faces, plus caps and wedges. The cycle shares its dodecahedron and its two icosahedra with the Lotus seed of the Chain of Karma, and each half of either structure fills its side of that dodecahedron exactly, so the two can be exchanged half by half at every scale. The cycle grows concentrically, one icosahedron per cycle (Nenrin growth), while the Lotus seed branches, 13 icosahedra per φ² step; the Lotus seed's 12 corner icosahedra straddle the shared dodecahedron, so they stay whole only when both halves are the Lotus seed's. The five cubes of the dodecahedron lie in the network's seams, and the five octahedra on the icosidodecahedron hold one icosahedron of edge 1 in Pacioli's golden position. Its outer shell, the rhombic triacontahedron, is the only other form found to branch like the Lotus seed (the Bodhi seed, described separately). The shells are the family of the Tsai-type cluster of icosahedral quasicrystals, here solid and exactly filled.

Checks. All 237 pieces of one cycle are pairwise free of overlap (separating axes), lie inside the outer icosahedron, and their total volume equals I(φ²) to 1e-12. The triacontahedron's edge is exactly ½√(45 − 18√5) = 1.0898138.

Terms: Ritsudō (律動, rhythm) for the six-shell cycle; Nenrin (年輪, tree rings) for its concentric growth. The icosidodecahedron as the twin form, the dual triangular structures, the triangles of rhombi, the fullerene transition, the last missing layer and all names are DICTO's. Computation and checking were done with Claude (Anthropic). Files: the paper (PDF) and its data, scripts, logs and renders (zip; also at https://github.com/DICTOR-Master/kaleidohedra).

metadata.title: Vajrayana
metadata.description:
Progenitors (DICTO DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23413184) set the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron O into the Spheres of Dharma in the dodecahedron's place and found an exact nine-station golden cycle, I ⊂ ID ⊂ O ⊂ rTI ⊂ TI ⊂ H ⊂ jtI ⊂ RT ⊂ I·φ³, closing on φ⁹ in volume. This companion asks where the dodecahedron went and what fills the cycle's loose steps. Every solid here is exact in ℚ(√5), and every nesting and volume is checked with remainder 0 unless marked float. The dodecahedron returns inside the icosidodecahedron, as the hull of DICTO's Cleo star: the icosahedron's 20 Cleo-Icos with 20 more turned outward have their tips exactly at (2/3)·D, and 82 pieces of four kinds fill that dodecahedron exactly. It touches both neighbours, both of its layers are a single kind of piece, and its dual closes the same step in the polar-reversed cycle. The full-height icosidodecahedron star gives a second member of the same family, the DICTO Palintriacontahedron, the rhombic triacontahedron turned inside out.
